summary: World Without Lights is a hands-on puzzle game that teaches how electrical circuits work through a fun rescue mission. In the story, all electricity on Earth has suddenly vanished, and people are going crazy without Wi-Fi. The player has only five minutes to save humanity by building a working circuit: using copper tape, LED lights, batteries and a battery holder, they must connect the lights around a handmade model of planet Earth until it lights up again. Our team built the model ourselves, with a papier-mâché globe, a starry base and a small astronaut watching over the planet. The game connects to a real NASA tool: satellites can see Earth’s lights from space and detect blackouts after disasters. By playing, kids learn how electricity flows through conductors like copper, how batteries provide energy, and why electricity is so important for our modern world.
details:
What it does and how it works. The player receives a set of materials: a cardboard base representing the world, copper tape to conduct electricity, LED lights, batteries and a battery holder. With a five-minute timer running, they must place the LEDs around the globe and connect them correctly with the copper tape to the batteries. If the circuit is built correctly, the lights turn on and humanity is saved. If time runs out, people “go crazy” without their internet.

What players learn. How a closed electrical circuit works, how electricity travels through conductive materials like copper, and how the energy stored in batteries makes LED lights turn on.

Benefits and intended impact. The game turns a science lesson into a hands-on challenge. Instead of just reading about circuits, players build one with their own hands, under time pressure, which makes the learning memorable and exciting.

Tools and materials. Papier-mâché for the globe, a cardboard base decorated as space, copper tape, blue LED lights, batteries, a battery holder, a toy astronaut, and Canva for the presentation.

Creativity. We combined a humorous story (a world in panic without Wi-Fi) with a real engineering challenge, and turned a simple circuit into a mission to save the planet.

Factors we considered. Choosing safe, low-voltage materials that kids can handle, setting a time limit that makes the game challenging but possible, and designing the circuit so the lights clearly show success.

Connection to space. From orbit, satellites can see the lights of cities at night. When a region loses power, it goes dark in these images. Our game imagines what would happen if the whole planet went dark, and lets players be the ones who bring the lights back.
